newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: American U.N. envoy says "jury still out" on Kabila.
newsitem.headline: American U.N. envoy says "jury still out" on Kabila.

text.p: American U.N. envoy Bill Richardson said on Monday Congolese President Laurent Kabila would find himself isolated if he failed to allow full access to a U.N. team being sent to investigate alleged massacres of Rwandan Hutu refugees in the former Zaire.
"The jury is still out on Kabila," Richardson said in an interview on public television's "Newshour."
"The next step has to be whether he allows full access for a U.N. investigative team ... to look at some very serious reports of massacres, of repatriation and refugee problems."

Richardson held talks with Kabila last month, shortly after the Congolese leader seized power from ousted President Mobutu Sese Seko, to stress the need for him to live up to promises of democratic government.

"The United States and the international community are prepared to help him, but only if he pursues significant political, economic and social reforms, and these human rights issues. If he doesn't, he is going to end up isolated," Richardson told the interviewer.

"He makes some positive steps, then he retreats into some negative steps," Richardson said. "I say let's wait until this U.N. team is in there ... Let's see how Kabila reacts to them. That's going to be his big testing ground.

"If he is reluctant to give them full access and plays games with the team, as he has in the past, and if he doesn't live up to the commitment he made to me and to Secretary-General (Kofi) Annan and the international commitment, then he is going to be isolated and he is not going to get help."
Asked whether Annan acted correctly in allowing Kabila to reject the U.N. chief's first choice to head the team, Richardson said Annan "was pragmatic and did the right thing."
A previous team "got into horrendous negotiations with Kabila" and each side lost credibility with the other.
If the new team did not receive full access, "there are going to be some very negative repercussions on Kabila and the way the international community can respond to help him."
